Have you ever zoned out on a Zoom call, then realised you’ve missed the last two minutes? I’ve been trying Wispr Flow’s Notetaker, which records and transcribes meetings in real time. You can ask it what you missed, search previous meetings for specific decisions, and use the transcripts with tools like ChatGPT and Claude to draft follow-up emails or messages. Very useful if, like me, you spend a lot of time in meetings, and even more time trying to remember what actually happened in them. Only about 1 in 10 menopausal women on Medicare uses vaginal estrogen, even though it cuts recurrent UTIs by more than half. That gap isn't a patient failure; it's the legacy of a boxed warning that sat on this drug for more than 20 years, built on data from a trial that never studied it. Laura Trujillo at USA TODAY reported today that the FDA is exploring making some vaginal estrogen products available over the counter, possibly as soon as mid-2027. It isn't approved yet: the FDA still needs evidence that women can use it safely without a clinician, and those studies are underway. The data behind the push is striking. I’ve been a physician for decades, and this one surprised me. Dense breasts don’t just make cancer harder to spot on a mammogram. They also raise your risk of breast cancer. The menopause guideline most OB-GYNs have practiced under was written in 2014, before the newest nonhormonal drugs existed and before the FDA changed the hormone therapy label. On October 15, ACOG replaced it: Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology (2026), covering hot flushes, sleep, and mood. Hormone therapy is strongly recommended for hot flushes and the sleep disruption they cause, started before 60 or within 10 years of menopause; continuing past 60 may be necessary if symptoms persist.
